Let me break this down with a couple of assumptions to get a little closer to reality.

Assumptions units sold per year ~ 200. Life cycle (years planning to sell before replaced / obsoleted by new model) 3 years. Mold tooling for custom back moulded plastic $25K - 40K (cant tell if there are special slides, but it looks simple). Metal stamp tooling for aluminum plate $5K. Amortized tooling per unit expecting 3 year pay back ~ $50 per unit. Unit is built in west instead of Asia due to quantities.

Bill Of Materials

Charger PCA ~ $50

Case with amortized tooling ~ $55

Fancy finger screws ~ $ 6

Misc Hardware and filler ~ $ 1

Assembly costs ~ $10

Testing ~ $ 5

You can buy them and receive them through the mail just like any other battery unless you're importing them from another country, in which customs will take a look to make sure they aren't cocaine filled tubes with a warning sticker on 'em. I'm not refuting anything else you've said, as it's all spot on - but storage and shipping of li ion batteries is pretty much a non-issue all over.

They may be OK depending on how they are classified, but below is some information from UPS and FEDEX with the regulation references for shipping. You also need to maintain charge on the batteries in storage if the monitoring and charging circuitry have any kind of significant leakage.

http://www.iata.org/whatwedo/cargo/dgr/Documents/lithium-battery-update.pdf

https://www.ups.com/media/news/en/intl_lithium_battery_regulations.pdf

http://images.fedex.com/downloads/jp/packagingtips/lithium/Lithium_Battery_Flow_Chart_2013.pdf

UPS and FedEx are private companies with their own limitations on shipping batteries, especially for international. I would never, ever, ever recommend using UPS or FedEx to transport batteries - the USPS does just fine in that regard. More often than not, UPS and FedEx will just hand it to the Post Office for delivery anyways.

You sound like someone who knows a thing or two - what did you mean by

"You also need to maintain charge on the batteries in storage if the monitoring and charging circuitry have any kind of significant leakage."?

Do you mean the batteries themselves, as stand alone cells not in an electronic device (like this battery pack in the video) need to be maintained with a full charge in storage? Or just ones in devices that might allow for long-term minor discharges?

UPS and FedEx are referencing the IATA link (first link), They just interpret it and spell it out for their customers.

As far as the storage issues, I am referring to the assemblies as shown in the unopened container in the video, or as part of a device. You will always have a discharge of some amount, the question is if its large enough to completely discharge in a significantly short amount of time. An example would be if your 4.6 AH battery pack in the assembly had a leakage discharge greater than 0.5 mA while in storage, it would be discharged from full charge in a year. That would mean that you need to go back and make sure you recharge that pack more than once a year. You would also want to make sure you are using a FIFO stocking distribution mechanism, to ensure you send your customer a reasonable charged and reliable unit. Now throw in the IATA requirement that you cannot ship it by air with more that 30% charge if your capacity is to big ...

As is stated before, its is difficult to get the individual cells by regular distribution means unless the cell manufacturer trusts you with being able to create protection that will not cause people to see their cell on fire. It may be easy for you to get plain cells through various back channel means, but the cell manufacturers would shut them down if they could. So even if they are making 18650 in bulk and selling 2.5 AH cells for less than $2 the companies that add the little protection board to the packs have a big markup because of the compliance to battery safety standards, and the trust of the cell manufacturer.

Wow, thanks for clearing some of that up for me. Good post.

Just, as a hobbyist, it's funny (funny-interesting, not funny-funny) to see people talk about it with different regards to the cells themselves. 18650 cells (by themselves) are demanding a big ol' chunk of market from RC, drone enthusiasts, high-discharge flashlights and headlamps and now the ecig/vapor market has them in very high demand. It's no secret that the battery manufacturers aren't very pleased with the increased demand - especially considering they've got their branding all over cells that (for all intents and purposes by the manufacturers) shouldn't be in consumer's hands. No one at LG Chem, for instance, likes seeing things in the news about LG batteries venting and causing equipment and physical damage.
